articles.title: South Korea unveils a roughly $900B AI and chip plan it calls a survival strategy - Crypto Briefing
articles.summary: South Korea unveils a roughly $900B AI and chip plan it calls a survival strategy  Crypto Briefing
articles.full_text:
Samsung and SK Hynix anchor a decade-long push into memory fabs, AI data centers and robotics
South Korea has put a price tag on its AI ambitions, and it is one of the largest national tech commitments on record.
On June 29, 2026, President Lee Jae Myung unveiled a public-private investment plan worth approximately $880–900 billion, or around 1,350 trillion won, to be deployed over the next decade.
Lee described the effort as a “national survival strategy.” He shared the stage with leaders from Samsung and SK Hynix.
Three bets, one decade
The plan rests on three flagship projects: memory chips, AI data centers, and physical AI and robotics.
Samsung and SK Hynix are committing approximately $518 billion, or 800 trillion won, to build new memory fabrication plants in the Gwangju region.
An additional approximately $52 billion is set aside for an HBM packaging hub. HBM stands for high-bandwidth memory, a design that stacks memory chips so they can feed data to AI processors quickly.
The second project is AI data centers. The plan calls for approximately $356 billion, or 550 trillion won, with a target of 8.4 GW of capacity by 2029.
AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
SK Group, GS Group and Naver are backing the data center buildout. The longer-range goal is more than 18 GW of AI data center capacity by 2035.
Seoul wants South Korea to rank among the top 3 global AI robot powers by 2030. It also plans to train 10,000 specialists in physical AI by the same year.
Superintelligence, in name more than in practice
The investment centers on computing power and semiconductor manufacturing, not on standalone ASI projects. The physical assets are concrete, while the superintelligence framing is aspirational.
Why Samsung and SK sit at the center
South Korea’s strategy leans on companies that already dominate parts of the memory market. Samsung, led by Jay Y. Lee, and SK, led by Chey Tae-won, are the key corporate figures attached to the plan.
The structure is a public-private partnership rather than a pure government spending bill. The state sets the direction and the targets, while corporate balance sheets supply much of the capital.
What this means
The HBM packaging hub deserves particular attention. High-bandwidth memory sits at the core of modern AI hardware, so a dedicated hub signals that Seoul wants to own more of the value chain, not just the raw memory chips.
Moving to 8.4 GW by 2029 and beyond 18 GW by 2035 implies a major expansion in electricity supply, and the plan’s credibility will partly depend on whether the power can be delivered on schedule.
The talent target may prove a quiet bottleneck. Fabs, data centers and robots all need skilled people, and 10,000 physical AI specialists by 2030 is a measurable milestone worth tracking.
The milestones to watch are groundbreaking progress on the Gwangju fabs, the 2029 data center capacity mark and the 2030 robotics and training goals.

articles.title: Former BOJ Board Member Says Japan No Longer Needs Stimulus, Sees Rate at 1.5% in December - bloomingbit
articles.summary: Former BOJ Board Member Says Japan No Longer Needs Stimulus, Sees Rate at 1.5% in December  bloomingbit
articles.full_text:
Summary
- Professor Asahi Noguchi said Japan no longer needs to support demand through fiscal and monetary policy.
- He said the BOJ may have little choice but to speed up rate hikes to keep the yen from weakening beyond 160 per dollar.
- Noguchi said he expects the BOJ to raise its benchmark interest rate to 1.50% from 1.25% in December, with a path to 1.75% and 2% depending on conditions.
Forecast Trend Report by Period
Japan no longer needs to support demand through fiscal or monetary policy, and the Bank of Japan is poised to raise its benchmark interest rate again in December, according to a former BOJ board member.
Asahi Noguchi, a Senshu University professor who served on the BOJ's policy board through March, said in an interview that underlying inflation is nearing the central bank's 2% target and wages have settled at a level consistent with 2% price growth, Reuters reported on October 5. Under those conditions, pursuing policies to lift demand further would be too risky, he said.
The BOJ raised interest rates in June and again in September. The pace of monetary-policy normalization has accelerated as inflationary pressure intensified, driven by higher import costs stemming from yen weakness and an energy-price shock tied to the war in Iran.
Noguchi said the BOJ would prefer gradual rate increases to avoid a recession, but may have little choice but to move faster to prevent the yen from weakening past 160 per dollar. Its biggest concern, though not something it would say publicly, is that the yen could fall beyond 160 against the dollar and trigger another jump in food prices, he said.
The yen is trading around 158 per dollar, close to the 160 level where markets see a rising chance of foreign-exchange intervention. Noguchi said the BOJ will probably hold rates steady this month as the likelihood of a U.S. rate increase in October has receded. He expects the central bank to lift its policy rate by 25 basis points in December, to 1.50% from 1.25%.
He also said the BOJ's policy rate could rise to 1.75%, and eventually 2%, depending on the extent of future Federal Reserve rate increases and developments in the Middle East. Japan's economy can absorb rates of up to 1.75%, he said. A move to 2%, however, could shock households and companies that have grown accustomed to ultra-low interest rates over a prolonged period.
Noguchi was previously a leading advocate of aggressive monetary easing. He joined the BOJ's policy board in 2021 and opposed both the end of negative interest rates in 2024 and a later rate increase to 0.25% that same year, but backed the two subsequent hikes.
He also said fiscal policy should move away from an expansionary stance now that Japan's output gap has turned positive. Excessive government spending could push up government bond yields and crowd out private-sector investment, he said.
Suehyeon Lee
shlee@bloomingbit.ioI'm reporter Suehyeon Lee, your Web3 Moderator.

articles.title: Japan’s population shrinks faster, but the government makes it harder for foreigners to live there - Fortune
articles.summary: Japan’s population shrinks faster, but the government makes it harder for foreigners to live there  Fortune
articles.full_text:
New census data over the past week showed Japan’s population shrank more quickly than in the prior tally. Also last week, the government rolled out tougher rules for foreign nationals who want to live in Japan.
While foreigners make up just 3.4% of Japan’s population, the share has increased to a record high and a political backlash has been building—even as the country also grapples with rapidly aging demographics and the need to find new workers to sustain economic growth.
On Tuesday, the latest five-year population survey detailed how stark Japan’s situation is. As of October 2025, the total population, including foreign residents, was 22.9 million, down 2.5% from five years earlier. The prior census in 2020 showed a dip of 0.7%.
The number of Japanese nationals revealed an even steeper decline of 3.5% to 119.1 million, following a 1.4% drop in the 2020 count.
Meanwhile, foreign residents jumped 40% to a record high of 3.84 million, and permanent residents climbed 17% to 947,125.
Like other wealthy economies in Asia, Japan’s birth rate has been below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman for decades, and the population has been in steady decline since around 2008.
At the same time, Japan is aging, and the percentage of people age 65 and older rose to 29.4% in 2025 from 28.5% in 2020. In fact, adult diapers have been outselling baby diapers since 2011.
The country is scrambling to find ways to encourage people to have more kids. For example, Tokyo’s metropolitan government launched a dating app to bring more couples together.
Tokyo also started a four-day workweek and partial leave policy for city workers to help those who are parents balance childcare and work.
By contrast, policies have turned more hostile when it comes to foreigners.
On Thursday, the Japanese government increased fees for permanent residency to $1,271 from $64 — a 2,000% jump that marks the largest increase in the country’s history. The cost for a five-year residence permit shot up to $475 from $38.
Japan also imposed more detailed requirements on income for permanent residents, who must now earn a minimum of $36,428 per year. And for the first time, applicants for permanent residency will be evaluated based on their Japanese language skills as well as their grasp of rules and customs.
On top of that, the government can revoke permanent residency for not meeting pension contribution obligations, failing to pay health insurance and taxes, and violating immigration law or the penal code.
The changes come as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has ushered in a more nationalist, right-wing stance.
On the global stage, that has meant taking a harder line against rivals like China and North Korea, while also bulking up Japan’s military.
Domestically, the pivot has translated to a crackdown on immigration and even tourism, drawing criticism that Takaichi is encouraging xenophobia. In July, the government hiked some tourist visa prices by more than 400%.
In a post on X ahead of the government’s new residency rules, Takaichi said many permanent residents could not maintain independent livelihoods.
“The government recognizes that, with the increasing number of foreign residents, there are citizens who feel anxiety and a sense of unfairness, and is addressing this by making ‘foreign policy’ more ‘orderly’ so that both citizens and foreigners can live safely and securely,” she wrote.

articles.title: Memory Chip Shortage Set to Persist Through 2028 as Micron Secures Orders - briefasia.com
articles.summary: Memory Chip Shortage Set to Persist Through 2028 as Micron Secures Orders  briefasia.com
articles.full_text:
Supply Commitments Signal Tight Market
The global memory chip shortage shows no sign of easing, with Micron Technology reporting that more than three-quarters of its production for fiscal 2027 has already been committed to buyers. The announcement underscores tight supply conditions that continue to favour the world's leading memory manufacturers, particularly South Korea's Samsung Electronics and SK hynix.
Micron disclosed on Wednesday that fiscal fourth-quarter revenue hit $54.23 billion, up nearly fivefold from $11.32 billion in the same period a year earlier. The figure exceeded analyst projections and marks the strongest quarterly performance in the company's history. The results reflect surging demand for memory components driven by artificial intelligence infrastructure, data centres, and consumer devices.
Korean Chipmakers Stand to Gain
The extended shortage strengthens the position of Samsung and SK hynix, which together control roughly 70 per cent of the global DRAM market and nearly half of the NAND flash segment. Both companies have reported robust earnings over the past year as memory prices climbed steadily from the trough reached in late 2023.
Samsung's semiconductor division posted operating profit of 6.6 trillion won (approximately $5 billion) in the second quarter of 2026, the highest in two years, while SK hynix recorded its third consecutive quarter of rising margins. Analysts expect both firms to maintain pricing discipline as supply remains constrained relative to demand.
The shortage stems from a combination of factors: capital expenditure cuts implemented during the 2023 downturn, longer lead times for advanced manufacturing nodes, and accelerating consumption tied to generative AI workloads. Micron's pre-sold inventory indicates that customers are locking in supply well ahead of delivery, a behaviour typically associated with prolonged scarcity.
Implications for the Chip Cycle
Memory markets have historically moved in pronounced cycles, with periods of oversupply driving down prices and prompting capacity reductions, followed by shortages that restore profitability. The current upcycle, which began in early 2024, has already lasted longer than many industry observers anticipated.
Micron's forward commitments suggest the cycle may extend into 2028, providing sustained revenue visibility for chipmakers and pricing leverage over original equipment manufacturers. That dynamic could support continued investment in next-generation technologies, including high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators and advanced packaging techniques.
For Samsung and SK hynix, the outlook offers an opportunity to recoup losses incurred during the previous downturn and fund transitions to smaller process nodes. Both companies have outlined plans to expand production of HBM3E, the latest iteration of high-bandwidth memory, which commands premium pricing and faces limited competition.
What Comes Next
Market participants will watch for signs of new capacity entering production and any shifts in customer ordering patterns. Micron's guidance for fiscal 2027, along with capital spending announcements from Samsung and SK hynix in the coming quarters, will provide further clarity on supply trajectories.
The shortage also carries implications for electronics manufacturers, which face higher input costs and potential allocation constraints. Companies reliant on memory-intensive products may need to adjust pricing or accept margin compression until supply conditions normalise.

articles.title: Yields rattle stocks as Korea eyes Samsung Q3 and key US data - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: Yields rattle stocks as Korea eyes Samsung Q3 and key US data - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
This week (the 5th–9th), Samsung Electronics(005930)'s preliminary third-quarter results will be released. The minutes of the Federal Reserve's September meeting (Fed) that could influence U.S. Government Bonds yields are also set to be made public. Expectations for corporations' earnings are expected to intersect with caution over macroeconomic variables such as Government Bonds yields and international oil prices.
Last week (Sept. 28–Oct. 2), the domestic stock market showed weak momentum due to a surge in U.S. Government Bonds yields. The U.S. 10-year Government Bonds yield rose intraday to 5.23% on the 1st, marking a 24-year record high. When market rates rise, they increase corporations' funding expense and discount rates, weighing on the stock market.
U.S. semiconductor company Micron reported strong results, but it only helped hold the market floor. Micron's fiscal year 2026 fourth-quarter revenue was $54.23 billion, beating market expectations ($51 billion), and its gross profit margin (GPM) was 87%, above the expected 85.2%. Guidance for the next quarter's revenue was set at $60 billion–$63 billion.
This week, investors are waiting for Samsung Electronics' preliminary third-quarter results due on the 8th. Many securities firm research centers are lowering their third-quarter operating profit forecasts for Samsung Electronics, citing the won-dollar exchange rate decline (won strength). According to Daishin Securities(003540), the consensus fell to 105 trillion won last week from 122.4 trillion won on Aug. 17.
However, expectations remain high that the semiconductor super-boom will continue. Korea's September exports rose 84% year over year to $120.9 billion, with semiconductor exports in particular surging 263%. Na Jeong-hwan, an NH Investment & Securities researcher, said, "There are short-term earnings concerns due to the stronger won, but the trend growth of semiconductor corporations continues."
Macro indicators and remarks by Fed officials that will determine the market's direction will also be released in succession. On the 5th (local time), the U.S. September Institute for Supply Management (ISM) services index will be announced. As services account for a large share of the U.S. economy, the index can show whether the expansionary trend continues.
On the 6th, a speech by New York Fed President John Williams is scheduled. On the 7th, the minutes of the U.S. September Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will be released. They will offer a look at the background to the September rate decision and Fed members' detailed views on additional tightening, serving as material to gauge the future rate path.
Some analysis suggests oil prices and interest rates could stabilize ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. Lee Kyung-min, a Daishin Securities researcher, said, "The probability of a blue sweep is around 62%–64% on Polymarket," and noted, "Given the increased political burden on the Trump administration, it may seek to resume negotiations with Iran and stabilize oil prices lower."
Meanwhile, share buybacks by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, which had served as major channels for large inflows into the main stock market, are expected to end soon. Samsung Electronics had bought back 14 trillion won as of the 1st, leaving only about 900 billion won of remaining capacity. SK hynix's cumulative buybacks total 32.0514 trillion won, accounting for 76.24% of the total planned purchases.

articles.title: Photolithography Equipment Market Forecast to 2035: AI and High-NA EUV Drive Growth - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: Photolithography Equipment Market Forecast to 2035: AI and High-NA EUV Drive Growth - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Photolithography Equipment market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global photolithography equipment market is the foundational enabler of semiconductor manufacturing, directly determining the pace of transistor miniaturization and chip performance. As of 2026, the market is defined by a bifurcated demand structure: leading-edge logic and memory producers are transitioning to extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and preparing for High-NA EUV insertion, while mature-node fabs continue to invest in deep ultraviolet (DUV) and i-line systems to serve automotive, industrial, and consumer applications. This report analyzes the market from 2026 to 2035, providing a data-driven outlook on system shipments, technology mix, regional dynamics, and competitive forces.
The analysis covers steppers, scanners, aligners, and EUV systems, with segmentation by application, wavelength, and value chain position. Key findings indicate that the market will grow at a robust CAGR, supported by secular demand for AI accelerators, advanced packaging, and the proliferation of connected devices. However, supply chain concentration, geopolitical tensions, and high capital costs present notable restraints. The report is designed for equipment manufacturers, component suppliers, foundries, IDMs, and investors seeking a consistent, transparent view of market dynamics and a clear definition of product scope.
The baseline scenario for the photolithography equipment market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates sustained growth, with a CAGR of 8.2%, reaching a market index of 220 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is anchored in the semiconductor industry's relentless pursuit of advanced nodes, where lithography accounts for an increasing share of wafer fab equipment spending. The transition to High-NA EUV, expected to enter high-volume manufacturing around 2028-2030, will drive a new wave of capital expenditure, particularly among leading logic and DRAM manufacturers.
Simultaneously, the expansion of mature node capacity, spurred by automotive electrification and industrial automation, will underpin steady demand for ArF immersion, KrF, and i-line systems. The market's value growth will also be supported by the rising complexity of systems, including advanced wafer stages, alignment systems, and control software. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will remain the dominant consumer, led by Taiwan, South Korea, and China, though China's share may be tempered by export controls and domestic substitution efforts. North America and Europe will see growth driven by fab construction incentives and the reshoring of semiconductor production.
The baseline scenario assumes no severe global recession and a stable geopolitical environment, though risks remain skewed to the downside due to trade restrictions and supply chain bottlenecks.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Rising demand for AI accelerators and high-performance computing chips, requiring advanced lithography nodes
- Commercialization of High-NA EUV systems enabling sub-2nm logic and advanced DRAM production
- Expansion of mature node capacity for automotive, industrial, and IoT applications, driving DUV and i-line equipment sales
- Growth in advanced packaging technologies, such as 2.5D and 3D ICs, necessitating dedicated lithography steps
- Increasing government incentives and fab construction in the U.S., Europe, and Japan to secure semiconductor supply chains
- Proliferation of flat panel display manufacturing, particularly for OLED and microLED, requiring high-resolution photolithography
Potential Growth Constraints
- High capital cost of EUV and High-NA EUV systems, limiting adoption to a few large manufacturers
- Geopolitical tensions and export controls restricting technology access to certain regions, notably China
- Supply chain concentration in critical components, such as optics and lasers, creating vulnerability to disruptions
- Cyclicality in semiconductor demand, leading to periodic oversupply and reduced capital expenditure
- Technical challenges in extending optical lithography beyond current limits, requiring significant R&D investment
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Semiconductor Fabrication (estimated share: 68%)
Semiconductor fabrication remains the dominant end-use sector for photolithography equipment, accounting for the majority of market value. The segment is characterized by a bifurcated demand pattern: leading-edge logic and memory manufacturers are aggressively adopting EUV and preparing for High-NA EUV to achieve sub-3nm nodes, driven by AI, cloud computing, and 5G. Meanwhile, mature node fabs (28nm and above) continue to invest in ArF immersion, KrF, and i-line systems to serve automotive, industrial, and consumer electronics. Through 2035, the segment will see a gradual shift toward higher-NA systems, with High-NA EUV becoming the standard for leading-edge production.
Demand-side indicators include wafer fab equipment spending, node transition rates, and capacity utilization at foundries and IDMs. The segment's growth is also supported by the increasing number of lithography layers per chip, as advanced packaging and 3D integration require additional patterning steps. Major players include TSMC, Samsung, Intel, and GlobalFoundries, who are the primary customers for advanced lithography systems. Current trend: Increasing share of EUV and High-NA EUV systems; steady demand for DUV in mature nodes.
Major trends: Transition to High-NA EUV for sub-2nm logic and advanced DRAM, Expansion of mature node capacity in China and other regions, Increasing lithography intensity per wafer due to multi-patterning and advanced packaging, Rising capital expenditure on EUV systems by leading foundries and IDMs, and Development of domestic lithography capabilities in China and other countries.
Representative participants: TSMC, Samsung Electronics, Intel Corporation, GlobalFoundries, Micron Technology, and SK Hynix.
Microelectromechanical Systems (MEMS) (estimated share: 8%)
The MEMS sector utilizes photolithography equipment for patterning microstructures on silicon wafers, with typical feature sizes ranging from 1 to 10 microns. Demand is driven by the proliferation of sensors in automotive (pressure, accelerometers, gyroscopes), consumer electronics (microphones, inertial sensors), and medical devices (lab-on-a-chip, biosensors). As MEMS devices become more complex and integrated with CMOS, the requirement for higher resolution and alignment accuracy is increasing, leading to greater adoption of i-line and KrF steppers. Through 2035, the segment will benefit from the growth of autonomous vehicles, smart manufacturing, and wearable health monitors.
Demand-side indicators include MEMS device shipments, automotive production volumes, and IoT connected device forecasts. The segment is less cyclical than leading-edge logic but is sensitive to consumer electronics cycles. Key equipment suppliers include SUSS MicroTec, EV Group, and Canon, while major MEMS manufacturers include Bosch, STMicroelectronics, and Texas Instruments. Current trend: Steady growth driven by automotive sensors, IoT, and medical devices; increasing use of i-line and KrF systems.
Major trends: Integration of MEMS with CMOS for smart sensors, Growing demand for MEMS in automotive safety and ADAS, Miniaturization of MEMS devices requiring advanced lithography, Expansion of MEMS foundries in Asia-Pacific, and Increasing use of nanoimprint lithography for MEMS patterning.
Representative participants: Robert Bosch GmbH, STMicroelectronics, Texas Instruments, Knowles Corporation, and Infineon Technologies.
Advanced Packaging (estimated share: 10%)
Advanced packaging has emerged as a critical enabler of high-performance computing, enabling the integration of multiple chiplets into a single package. Photolithography equipment is used for creating redistribution layers (RDLs), microbumps, and through-silicon vias (TSVs), requiring thick photoresist processing and high-accuracy alignment. The segment is growing rapidly, driven by AI, data centers, and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Through 2035, the demand for advanced packaging lithography will be fueled by the need for higher interconnect density and the adoption of fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) and 3D stacking.
Demand-side indicators include advanced packaging capacity expansions, chiplet adoption rates, and HBM production volumes. Equipment requirements include i-line and KrF steppers with thick resist capabilities, as well as mask aligners. Major players in this segment include ASE Technology, Amkor Technology, and TSMC, while equipment suppliers include Canon, Nikon, and SUSS MicroTec. Current trend: Rapid growth due to 2.5D/3D ICs, chiplets, and heterogeneous integration; demand for thick resist and alignment systems.
Major trends: Shift from wafer-level to panel-level packaging for cost reduction, Increasing use of hybrid bonding requiring sub-micron alignment, Growth of chiplet-based designs in high-performance computing, Expansion of advanced packaging capacity in Taiwan, South Korea, and China, and Development of new photoresists for thick film applications.
Representative participants: ASE Technology Holding, Amkor Technology, TSMC, Samsung Electronics, and Intel Corporation.
Flat Panel Display (FPD) Manufacturing (estimated share: 9%)
Flat panel display manufacturing uses photolithography equipment for patterning thin-film transistors (TFTs) and color filters on glass substrates. articles.title: Rising prices, weak spending put Japan's policymakers in tight spot - news.cgtn.com
articles.summary: Rising prices, weak spending put Japan's policymakers in tight spot  news.cgtn.com
articles.full_text:
At a chain store in Tokyo, the Japanese capital, a notice announcing price adjustments on selected items is hard to miss.
These days, price hikes not only rank among the most talked-about topics in Japanese media but are also keenly felt in daily life, from household goods to food and from supermarkets to restaurants.
A customer shops for groceries at a supermarket in Tokyo, Japan, July 24, 2026. /VCG
Rising prices, weak consumption
According to a survey released by Japanese research firm Teikoku Databank, more than 3,000 food and beverage items in the country are set to go up in price in October, with the full-year tally for 2026 expected to top 20,000.
Data recently released by the Bank of Japan (BOJ) showed that the consumer price index excluding institutional factors rose 2.6% year on year in August, overshooting the central bank's 2% price stability target.
With prices climbing across the board, spending is showing signs of slowing.
Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's economy, was essentially flat in the second quarter.
As of July, inflation-adjusted household spending had declined year on year for eight consecutive months.
"Rising prices are eroding real purchasing power, and private consumption is likely to stagnate further going forward," said Taro Saito, an economist at NLI Research Institute.
Weak consumer demand is also weighing on corporate earnings. Shingo Ide, chief equity strategist at NLI Research Institute, noted that with costs broadly on the rise, companies that cannot pass them on to customers through higher prices will face sustained pressure on their profit margins, putting their businesses under considerable strain.
Large Japanese companies with strong pricing power still have some room to offset rising costs through price increases, but for the country's many small and medium-sized businesses, raising prices is far from easy.
Take ramen shops, a staple of Japan's dining scene, for example. According to Tokyo Shoko Research, bankruptcies among ramen shops jumped 44.4% year on year in the first half of 2026, pushing the number of failures to a record high for the period.
Persistently rising costs for ingredients and utilities have forced many ramen shop owners to raise prices, but as consumers grow more cautious about spending, higher prices risk driving customers away.
For many small restaurant operators in Japan, striking a balance between covering elevated costs and keeping customers coming through the door has become a headache.
Abandoned and vacant storefronts with weathered facades and damaged display windows in Hakodate, Hokkaido, Japan, June 18, 2026. /VCG
Limited policy toolkit
With rising prices eating into household purchasing power and business costs continuing to climb, Japan's economic policymakers face an increasingly stark dilemma.
On monetary policy, the BOJ finds itself in a bind. The risk that a weaker yen and inflated import costs will push prices up further has not gone away, giving the central bank reason to continue with its tightening cycle.
At the same time, with signs of softening consumption already emerging, raising interest rates too quickly could dampen economic activity.
Recent movements in the yen have added complexity to the BOJ's policy calculus. Even after joint intervention by Japan and the United States in the currency market, the yen has continued to face selling pressure.
A recent Reuters poll found that more than two-thirds of economists surveyed believe the joint intervention has had only a limited effect, merely postponing rather than resolving the deeper problems facing the yen. Against this backdrop, market expectations of a BOJ rate hike have gained noticeable momentum.
At its September policy meeting, the central bank raised its key interest rate to 1.25%. However, because the US Federal Reserve also hiked its target federal funds rate, the interest rate gap between Japan and the United States narrowed only modestly, and the yen failed to sustain a meaningful rebound.
According to multiple Japanese media reports, US President Donald Trump recently voiced concerns about the yen's weakness.
The BOJ, for its part, is keeping a close eye on the inflationary impact of a weaker currency.
"If the yen weakens further and economic indicators point to mounting price pressures, the likelihood of a BOJ rate hike in October will increase," said Eiji Maeda, president of Chibagin Research Institute and a former BOJ executive director.
A pedestrian passes by an electronic stock board showing Japan's Nikkei index at a securities firm in Tokyo, Japan, September 29, 2026. /VCG
Kyohei Morita, chief economist at Nomura Securities, said the fiscal policy of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government has pushed up inflation expectations, deepening market concerns that the BOJ is falling behind the curve.
On the fiscal side, the Takaichi government's strategy of "responsible and proactive" public finances is running up against the hard reality of limited fiscal space.
A Reuters poll found that 89% of economists surveyed expect the government's fiscal policy to drive the yen lower, with markets particularly focused on how measures such as a food tax cut and expanded investment will be funded.
Amid growing concerns over fiscal sustainability, the yield on the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond, a barometer of long-term interest rates, rose to as high as 3.115% at one stage on September 25, its highest level since August 1996.
Japan's government debt has long been high relative to GDP, and as interest rates climb, that debt load is turning into a more immediate interest burden.
According to the Nikkei newspaper, the Ministry of Finance's budget request for fiscal 2027, which runs from April 2027 to March 2028, puts debt-servicing costs at 36.64 trillion yen (about $232 billion), including 16.59 trillion yen in interest payments, both record highs.
Ultimately, Japan's current economic troubles go beyond a simple rise in prices. They stem from the interplay of shrinking household purchasing power, rising business costs and mounting fiscal pressure, each pulling against the others. When it comes to reconciling price stability, growth and debt control, Japan's policymakers have limited room to maneuver.

articles.title: MU, SNDK, DRAM Fall Sharply From Record Highs: Korean Market Crashes 10% Crash On SK Hynix, Samsung Pullback - Stocktwits
articles.summary: MU, SNDK, DRAM Fall Sharply From Record Highs: Korean Market Crashes 10% Crash On SK Hynix, Samsung Pullback  Stocktwits
articles.full_text:
U.S. memory chip stocks tumbled from record highs in Tuesday’s premarket trading, caught in a broader tech selloff that began Monday and spilled over into Asian markets overnight.
SanDisk shares dropped 9.3%, while Micron stock declined 8.4%. Seagate and Western Digital shares declined over 7% each, and the Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) was down 13%.
South Korea’s Kospi closed 10% lower on Tuesday, with SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics both sliding more than 12%. At one point, the trading was suspended for 20 minutes, a measure to avoid a runaway slide in the market.
In fact, artificial intelligence-linked stocks tumbled across Japan and European markets.
SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron are the top three holdings of DRAM. MU, SNDK, and DRAM closed at record highs on Monday.
Investor confidence in some of the market’s top-performing technology names showed signs of weakening in Monday’s U.S. session, as SpaceX shares declined and traders looked ahead to memory-chip maker Micron Technology’s earnings report due Wednesday.
S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures fell early Tuesday after a sell-off in tech giants dragged down the broad market index. After rallying sharply in recent months, memory stocks were the top focus for retail investors as they debated whether the premarket drops were a temporary blip or the start of a correction period.
On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment from DRAM shifted to ‘bullish’ from ‘neutral,’ while that for WDC dipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘extremely bullish.’
The sentiment remained ‘bearish’ for MU, SNDK, and ‘bullish’ for STX.
“$SNDK Institutions and insiders are taking all the profits. $MU $DRAM,” said a trader.
Another wrote: “$SNDK these inflated memory names sucked the air out of more deserving AI names like NVDA…let’s just hope the memory crash doesn’t take down the legitimate AI plays with it.”`
The drop is not a crash, contended a trader. “$MU Kospi. It’s more sell the news / profit-taking after an extreme rally than a full crash,” they said.
Memory-chip stocks have surged over the past year on AI-driven demand for data centers. While companies and analysts still expect strong growth ahead, investors are increasingly debating how much of that optimism is already priced into shares and how much upside remains.

articles.title: BOJ December Rate Hike to 1.5% Likely, Says Former Board Member Noguchi - IndexBox
articles.summary: BOJ December Rate Hike to 1.5% Likely, Says Former Board Member Noguchi  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Japan no longer requires expansionary fiscal and monetary policies designed to stimulate demand, according to Asahi Noguchi, a former Bank of Japan board member, as reported by Reuters. Noguchi, a reflationist academic who served at the central bank until March, told the news agency that he expects another interest rate increase by the BOJ in December.
His comments underscore a broader shift in thinking among former advocates of heavy spending and loose monetary policy, driven by years of rising inflation and wages. Noguchi said underlying inflation is close to the BOJ's 2% target and that wages are becoming embedded at levels consistent with 2% inflation, making demand-boosting policies too risky.
After years of cautious movement on policy normalisation, the BOJ accelerated its rate increases with hikes in June and September. According to Noguchi, an energy shock linked to the Iran war compounded price pressures from rising import costs caused by a weak yen. While the BOJ likely preferred a gradual approach to avoid another economic downturn, Noguchi said it had little choice but to move faster to prevent undesirable yen declines.
He noted that it is difficult for the BOJ to act slowly when other central banks are shifting toward rate increases amid global inflationary pressures. Noguchi added that the BOJ is mostly concerned about the risk of the yen sliding below 160 against the dollar, which would trigger a fresh wave of food inflation, though he said the central bank would not state this openly.
A weak yen has become a problem for Japan by raising import costs. The yen has traded around 158, near the 160 level that markets view as increasing the chance of yen intervention, as prospects of near-term US rate hikes strengthen the dollar.
Noguchi said receding prospects of a US rate hike in October will likely allow the BOJ to hold steady this month, but he sees a good chance the central bank will raise its policy rate to 1.5% from the current 1.25% in December.
Phasing Out Reflationism
The BOJ could eventually lift its policy rate to 1.75% or even 2%, depending on how far its US counterpart raises rates and on developments in the Middle East conflict, according to Noguchi. He said a hike to 1.75% is unlikely to hurt the economy, while an increase to 2% could be risky because it might shock households and firms long accustomed to ultra-low borrowing costs.
Noguchi said that with so much uncertainty about how rate hikes affect the economy, the BOJ probably wants to proceed very slowly, but market forces will not allow it to do so.

articles.title: Foreign Investors Dump 20 Trillion Won in Korean Stocks in a Month - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Foreign Investors Dump 20 Trillion Won in Korean Stocks in a Month  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
Foreign investors sold a net 20 trillion won worth of KOSPI shares over the past month or so, with the selling concentrated in Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK hynix (000660.KS). The two chipmakers alone accounted for more than 17 trillion won in net sales, pulling down foreign ownership in both. Analysts, however, say the pace of selling matters more than the cumulative total, noting that it has been easing. They expect foreign buying could return if third-quarter earnings confirm a solid chip market and profit growth.
Foreign investors sold a net 20.305 trillion won on the KOSPI between the 1st of last month and the 2nd of this month, according to the Korea Exchange on the 5th. The figure includes after-market trading, which launched on the 15th of last month. Foreigners were net buyers on only seven of the 22 trading sessions in that period. On the 28th of last month alone, net selling topped 3 trillion won. Foreign holdings now account for 39.66% of total KOSPI market capitalization, down from earlier levels.
The selling was concentrated in large-cap chip stocks. Net selling in SK hynix was the largest at 12.009 trillion won, followed by Samsung Electronics at 5.186 trillion won. Combined net sales of 17.195 trillion won in the two stocks amounted to about 85% of total foreign net selling on the KOSPI.
Foreign ownership ratios fell in tandem. SK hynix stood at 49.76% as of the 2nd of this month, the lowest in about three years and four months since May 15, 2023, when it was 49.46%. Samsung Electronics slid to 46.40% on the 30th of last month before edging up to 46.41% on the 2nd.
The selling reflects continued profit-taking after a steep rally in large-cap chip stocks in the first half. Uncertainty over the protracted war between the United States and Iran, along with rising interest rates in the U.S., Europe and other major economies, also appears to have weighed on sentiment.
The intensity of the selling has eased somewhat this month. Foreign investors bought a net 243 billion won on the KOSPI on the 1st, and while they returned to net selling on the 2nd, the amount was limited to 190 billion won. That is why analysts say investors should watch the easing selling pressure rather than judge the market's direction solely on whether foreign selling continues.
Han Ji-young, an analyst at Kiwoom Securities, said foreign net selling on the KOSPI is at its highest level since the start of the year, but monthly net purchase figures show the intensity of that selling has weakened over time. "At this point, reading the streak of foreign net selling as a signal of a trend break and cutting equity exposure on rebounds should be a lower priority," the analyst said. "Investors need to maintain their exposure to Korean equities, centered on key sectors such as semiconductors, on the view that foreign investors are likely to return as net buyers once macro risks pass their peak."
Chipmakers' earnings are seen as the variable that will determine fund flows from here. Micron Technology, the first of the three global memory makers to report, posted better-than-expected results on the 30th of last month. Samsung Electronics is scheduled to release preliminary third-quarter earnings around the 8th of this month. If chipmakers can demonstrate a firm market through their results and improve visibility on future profits, that could support a return of foreign money to the Korean market, analysts said.
